summary: Specifies the encoding of CCNx messages in a TLV packet format, including TLV types for each message element and the value encodings. Semantics follow the CCNx Semantics specification. It comes from the Information Centric Networking research group and is experimental.

plainLanguage.summary: The exact way CCNx messages are written out as bytes, with labeled boxes that hold each piece.

questions: what is an interest in ccnx
subtitle: How CCNx requests and responses are laid out as bytes: an 8-byte fixed header and nested type-length-value boxes.

tldr.problem: CCNx routes requests by hierarchical name instead of by endpoint address, and RFC 8569 describes its messages without saying how they look on the wire. Every forwarder on the path has to parse and check each packet.
tldr.mechanism: Packets start with an 8-byte fixed header, then optional hop-by-hop headers, then a CCNx Message built from nested TLVs that each have a fixed 2-byte Type and 2-byte Length. Optional validation TLVs carry a checksum, MAC or signature.
tldr.outcome: The fixed-size fields avoid alias encodings and keep per-hop validation cheap. The RFC is an Experimental IRTF document, not an IETF standard, and it has been updated by RFC 9510.

today: RFC 8609 is an Experimental RFC from the IRTF, not an IETF standard, and it is updated by RFC 9510. The text itself says the specification may change in the future.

sections.title: What This Specification Covers
sections.content:
CCNx is a network protocol that uses a hierarchical name to forward requests and to match responses to requests. It does not use endpoint addresses, although the Internet Protocol underneath does. An Interest asks for a Content Object with a matching name, and a Content Object is the data sent back. The meaning of these messages lives in RFC 8569; this document only defines the encoding.

The RFC specifies the packet format, the message TLV format, the TLV types and the value encoding for each. It uses a Type-Length-Value scheme with a fixed 2-byte T and a fixed 2-byte L, so there are 65,536 possible types and values up to 64 KiB. Jumbo packets beyond 64 KiB are not supported.
sections.plainLanguage: CCNx asks for things by name, like asking a library for a book title instead of a shelf number. This RFC is the label-making guide for the messages.

sections.title: The Packet and Its Fixed Header
sections.content:
A CCNx packet is an 8-byte fixed header, then optional hop-by-hop header TLVs, then the packet payload. The payload is the protocol message itself, optionally followed by a ValidationAlgorithm TLV and a ValidationPayload TLV. Because the payload is self-sufficient, a network stack can drop the headers and work only on the embedded message.

The fixed header holds Version (which MUST be 1), PacketType, PacketLength, HeaderLength (minimum 8) and some type-specific bytes. The packet type says how to forward the packet: PT_INTEREST for a request, PT_CONTENT for a response and PT_RETURN for an Interest Return.

An Interest header adds a HopLimit. The originator may use any value up to 255, each node decrements it, and if it reaches 0 the Interest MUST NOT be forwarded off the node. An Interest Return keeps the original Interest bytes and only changes the packet type and sets a ReturnCode, so no extra bytes are needed to send it back. A return code of 0 MUST NOT be used.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet starts with a small cover sheet that says what kind of packet it is and how long it is. An Interest also carries a countdown so it cannot wander the network forever.

sections.title: TLVs, Vendor Data, Hashes and Hop-by-Hop Headers
sections.content:
Every TLV is a 16-bit Type and a 16-bit Length, then the value. Length counts only the value, and it MAY be zero. TLVs nest, and type values are context dependent, so the same number can mean different things in different containers. Types 0x1000 to 0x1FFF are reserved for experimental use.

A T_PAD TLV can pad out to word alignment and must be zeros, but a Name MUST NOT contain padding. A T_ORG TLV carries vendor-specific data, starting with a 3-byte organization number from the IANA Private Enterprise Numbers registry. Hash values use a nested form (hash type, length, value) so a router can compare them bit by bit without understanding the hash function. Every entity MUST support T_SHA-256 and MAY support others such as T_SHA-512.

A Link is a name plus an optional KeyId restriction and an optional ContentObjectHash restriction. It is essentially the body of an Interest.

Hop-by-hop headers can change as a packet travels, so they sit outside the signed and hashed part. They are unordered, and no meaning may be attached to their order. Three are defined.

  • T_INTLIFE, the Interest Lifetime, is how long an Interest should stay pending at an intermediate node, in milliseconds. A value of 0 means no Content Object is expected, so a forwarder could skip creating a pending-interest entry.
  • T_CACHETIME, the Recommended Cache Time, is a 64-bit millisecond timestamp. It only guides the cache and may be ignored, unlike the ExpiryTime inside the message, which must be obeyed. Since it is not signed, a producer can re-issue a signed object with a new value without re-signing.
  • T_MSGHASH, the Message Hash, lets an operator compute a hash once at a border device so inner devices can check a hash restriction without recomputing it. It is unprotected, so it is only useful inside a trusted domain.
sections.plainLanguage:
Each box has a label saying what it is and a number saying how long it is, and boxes can sit inside bigger boxes. Some labels are saved for tests and for company-specific use.

These are sticky notes on the outside of the parcel. Post offices can change or add them, because they are not part of the sealed contents.

sections.title: The CCNx Message TLV
sections.content:
The message TLV sits between the hop-by-hop headers and the validation TLVs. Its type, T_INTEREST or T_OBJECT, tells Interests and Content Objects apart. Inside it come the Name TLV first, then optional message TLVs, then an optional T_PAYLOAD.

A Name is a list of segments such as T_NAMESEGMENT. A zero-length Name means ccnx:/, the default route. The RFC encodes ccnx:/foo/bar/hi as a Name of length 20 holding three segments of lengths 3, 3 and 2. There are also 4096 application-specific segment types, and T_IPID, the Interest Payload ID, a segment that identifies an Interest's payload, for example by hashing it.

An Interest can add T_KEYIDRESTR to accept only objects signed by a given key, and T_OBJHASHRESTR to accept only the object with a given hash (which SHOULD be a 32-byte T_SHA-256). A Content Object can add T_PAYLDTYPE (data, key or link; data if missing) and T_EXPIRY, a 64-bit millisecond timestamp after which a cache or end system should not answer with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Inside the packet is the actual question or answer. A question has a name and maybe a rule like only accept an answer from this person. An answer has the name, what kind of thing it is and when it goes stale.

sections.title: Validation
sections.content:
Both Interests and Content Objects may say how to validate them, using two top-level TLVs. T_VALIDATION_ALG names the method and carries the data needed, and T_VALIDATION_PAYLOAD carries the result, such as a CRC32C code or an RSA signature. The protected range covers the message TLV and the ValidationAlgorithm TLV.

The defined types are T_CRC32C (a message integrity check that needs no extra data), T_HMAC-SHA256 (a MAC for parties that already share a secret key), T_RSA-SHA256 and the elliptic-curve types T_EC-SECP-256K1 and T_EC-SECP-384R1. Signatures need a KeyId and a way to find the public key. Optional data includes a public key, an X.509 certificate, a KeyLink and a signature time.

An Interest would most likely only use a MIC type of validation.
sections.plainLanguage: Validation is the seal on the parcel. A simple seal shows nobody crushed it, and a fancy one proves exactly who sent it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CCNx supports message authentication through signatures or MACs, and a MIC can be used instead. It specifies no encryption envelope, leaving that to a higher-layer protocol, and it leaves key trust to applications.

Applications should choose carefully when to put a ValidationAlgorithm on an Interest. MICs are cheap, but MACs and signatures are costly and could open a computational DoS attack surface. Simply adding a signature does not make an Interest secure, and secured Interests need replay protection.

The fixed 2-byte T and L were chosen to avoid aliases, where the same value could be encoded in different lengths. Aliases would force validation of every field at every hop or make packet filters complicated. An Interest Return has no authenticator from the previous hop, so its payload should only be used locally to match an Interest. Caches must follow the rules in RFC 8569 to avoid poisoning.
sections.plainLanguage: A seal helps, but it does not make a message safe on its own. Use cheap seals for everyday messages, because checking fancy seals takes time that someone could abuse.

fields.name: PacketLength
fields.desc: Total octets of the packet including all headers.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: No flags defined, so MUST be 0.

fields.name: HeaderLength
fields.desc: Fixed header plus hop-by-hop headers; minimum 8.
